# The Two Searches

*MN 26, the Pāsarāsi Sutta — set 1, Before Any Doctrine*

## About this text

Most of these texts are the Buddha teaching. This one is the Buddha
describing what happened to him — leaving home, studying under two accomplished
meditation teachers, getting everything they had to offer, and concluding it
was not enough.

The frame he sets up is a distinction between two kinds of searching. One goes
after things that are themselves subject to ageing, sickness and death; the
other goes after what is not. Put that plainly and it sounds obvious. The
force of it is in noticing how much of an ordinary life is the first kind.

Read this early, before the vocabulary gets technical. It is the human anchor
under everything that follows: someone tried the available options, found them
insufficient, and kept going.

## The Setting

At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove,
Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery.

Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking bowl and robe, set
out for Sāvatthī on alms-round. Several bhikkhus went to Venerable Ānanda and
said: "Reverend Ānanda, it has been a long time since we heard a teaching-talk
face to face with the Buddha. It would be good if we could hear one."

"Then, reverends, go to the brahmin Rammaka's hermitage. Perhaps you will get
to hear a teaching-talk face to face with the Buddha."

"Yes, reverend," they replied.

Then, after the meal, returning from alms-round, the Buddha addressed
Venerable Ānanda: "Come, Ānanda, let us go to the Eastern Monastery, the
stilt-longhouse of Migāra's mother, for the day's dwelling."

"Yes, Bhante," Ānanda replied.

So the Buddha went with Ānanda to the stilt-longhouse of Migāra's mother
for the day's dwelling. In the late afternoon, the Buddha came out of
seclusion and addressed Ānanda: "Come, Ānanda, let us go to the eastern gate
to bathe."

"Yes, Bhante," Ānanda replied.

So the Buddha went with Ānanda to the eastern gate to bathe. Having
bathed and emerged from the water, he stood in a single robe, drying his
limbs. Then Venerable Ānanda said: "Bhante, the brahmin Rammaka's hermitage
is nearby. It is delightful, beautiful. Bhante, may the Buddha visit it
out of compassion."

The Buddha consented with silence.

## The Two Searches

He went to the brahmin Rammaka's hermitage. At that time several bhikkhus were
sitting together there talking about the Dhamma. The Buddha stood outside
the door waiting for the talk to end. When he knew it had ended, he cleared his
throat and knocked on the door-panel. The bhikkhus opened the door. The Buddha entered, sat down on the seat spread out, and addressed the bhikkhus:
"Bhikkhus, what were you sitting talking about just now? What conversation was
left unfinished?"

"Bhante, a teaching-talk about the Buddha himself was left unfinished when
the Buddha arrived."

"Good, bhikkhus! This is fitting for gentlemen who have gone forth from home
into homelessness out of confidence — that you would sit together talking about
the Dhamma. When gathered together, bhikkhus, you should do one of two things:
talk about the Dhamma, or keep noble silence.

Bhikkhus, there are two searches: the noble search and the ignoble search.

And what is the ignoble search? Here, someone who is themselves subject to
birth seeks only what is subject to birth. Being themselves subject to aging,
they seek only what is subject to aging. Being themselves subject to sickness,
they seek only what is subject to sickness. Being themselves subject to death,
they seek only what is subject to death. Being themselves subject to sorrow,
they seek only what is subject to sorrow. Being themselves subject to
corruption, they seek only what is subject to corruption.

And what should be described as subject to birth? Partners and children,
bhikkhus, are subject to birth; male and female servants are subject to birth;
goats and sheep are subject to birth; chickens and pigs are subject to birth;
elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are subject to birth; gold and silver are
subject to birth. These are supports subject to birth. Someone who is tied,
infatuated, and immersed in these — being themselves subject to birth — seeks
only what is subject to birth.

And what should be described as subject to aging? Partners and children,
bhikkhus, are subject to aging; male and female servants are subject to aging;
goats and sheep are subject to aging; chickens and pigs are subject to aging;
elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are subject to aging; gold and silver are
subject to aging. These are supports subject to aging. Someone who is tied,
infatuated, and immersed in these — being themselves subject to aging — seeks
only what is subject to aging.

And what should be described as subject to sickness? Partners and children,
bhikkhus, are subject to sickness; male and female servants are subject to
sickness; goats and sheep are subject to sickness; chickens and pigs are
subject to sickness; elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are subject to
sickness. These are supports subject to sickness. Someone who is tied,
infatuated, and immersed in these — being themselves subject to sickness —
seeks only what is subject to sickness.

And what should be described as subject to death? Partners and children,
bhikkhus, are subject to death; male and female servants are subject to death;
goats and sheep are subject to death; chickens and pigs are subject to death;
elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are subject to death. These are supports
subject to death. Someone who is tied, infatuated, and immersed in these —
being themselves subject to death — seeks only what is subject to death.

And what should be described as subject to sorrow? Partners and children,
bhikkhus, are subject to sorrow; male and female servants are subject to
sorrow; goats and sheep are subject to sorrow; chickens and pigs are subject to
sorrow; elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are subject to sorrow. These are
supports subject to sorrow. Someone who is tied, infatuated, and immersed in
these — being themselves subject to sorrow — seeks only what is subject to
sorrow.

And what should be described as subject to corruption? Partners and children,
bhikkhus, are subject to corruption; male and female servants are subject to
corruption; goats and sheep are subject to corruption; chickens and pigs are
subject to corruption; elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are subject to
corruption; gold and silver are subject to corruption. These are supports
subject to corruption. Someone who is tied, infatuated, and immersed in these —
being themselves subject to corruption — seeks only what is subject to
corruption. This is the ignoble search.

And what is the noble search? Here, someone who is themselves subject to birth,
having seen the danger in what is subject to birth, seeks nibbāna — the supreme
security from the yoke, free from birth. Being themselves subject to aging,
having seen the danger in what is subject to aging, they seek nibbāna — the
supreme security from the yoke, free from aging. Being themselves subject to
sickness, having seen the danger in what is subject to sickness, they seek
nibbāna — the supreme security from the yoke, free from sickness. Being
themselves subject to death, having seen the danger in what is subject to
death, they seek nibbāna — the supreme security from the yoke, free from
death. Being themselves subject to sorrow, having seen the danger in what is
subject to sorrow, they seek nibbāna — the supreme security from the yoke,
free from sorrow. Being themselves subject to corruption, having seen the
danger in what is subject to corruption, they seek nibbāna — the supreme
security from the yoke, free from corruption. This is the noble search.

## The Bodhisatta's Own Search

Bhikkhus, before my awakening — when I was still unawakened but intent on
awakening — I too, being myself subject to birth, sought only what was subject
to birth. Being myself subject to aging, sickness, death, sorrow, and
corruption, I sought only what was subject to those things.

Then it occurred to me: 'Why do I, being myself subject to birth, seek only
what is subject to birth? Being myself subject to aging, sickness, death,
sorrow, and corruption, why do I seek only what is subject to those things?
What if I were to see the danger in what is subject to birth, aging, sickness,
death, sorrow, and corruption, and seek nibbāna — the supreme security from
the yoke, free from birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, and corruption?'

## Going Forth

Some time later, while I was still young, with pristine black hair, endowed
with the blessing of youth, in the prime of life — though my mother and father
wished otherwise, weeping with tear-streaked faces — I shaved off hair and
beard, put on ochre robes, and went forth from home into homelessness.

## Āḷāra Kālāma

Having gone forth in search of the good, seeking the supreme resting-place of
peace, I went to Āḷāra Kālāma and said: "Reverend Kālāma, I wish to live the
spiritual life in this teaching and training."

Āḷāra Kālāma replied: "Stay, venerable. This teaching is such that a sensible
person can soon realize their own teacher's tradition with their own higher
knowing, live having entered into it, and make it known."

I quickly mastered that teaching. Then it occurred to me: 'Āḷāra Kālāma does
not proclaim "I live having realized this teaching with my own higher knowing,
having entered into it" by mere faith alone — surely he lives knowing and
seeing this teaching.' So I approached Āḷāra Kālāma and asked: "Reverend
Kālāma, up to what point do you proclaim that you have realized this teaching
with your own higher knowing and entered into it?"

When I said this, he declared the sphere of nothingness.

Then it occurred to me: 'It is not only Āḷāra Kālāma who has confidence — I
too have confidence. It is not only Āḷāra Kālāma who has energy, remembering,
mental composure, and discernment — I too have these. What if I were to make
the effort to realize the teaching that Āḷāra Kālāma proclaims he has realized
with his own higher knowing?'

Soon enough, I too realized that teaching with my own higher knowing and
entered into it. I went to Āḷāra Kālāma and said: "Reverend Kālāma, is it up
to this point that you have realized this teaching with your own higher knowing
and entered into it?"

"It is up to this point, reverend."

"I too, reverend, have realized this teaching with my own higher knowing up to
this point and live having entered into it."

"We are fortunate, reverend — how very fortunate — to see such a venerable as
yourself as a fellow practitioner! The teaching that I have realized with my
own higher knowing and entered into — that you live having realized with your
own higher knowing. The teaching that you live having realized with your own
higher knowing — that I have realized and made known. What I know, you know;
what you know, I know. As I am, so are you; as you are, so am I. Come now,
reverend — let us both lead this community together."

And so Āḷāra Kālāma, my teacher, placed me his student on equal footing with
himself and honored me with high honor.

Then it occurred to me: 'This teaching does not lead to disenchantment, fading,
cessation, calming, higher knowing, awakening, or nibbāna — only as far as
rebirth in the sphere of nothingness.'

Not finding this teaching satisfying, I turned away from it and left.

## Uddaka Rāmaputta

Still in search of the good, seeking the supreme resting-place of peace, I
went to Uddaka, son of Rāma, and said: "Reverend, I wish to live the spiritual
life in this teaching and training."

Uddaka, son of Rāma, replied: "Stay, venerable. This teaching is such that a
sensible person can soon realize their own teacher's tradition with their own
higher knowing, live having entered into it, and make it known."

I quickly mastered that teaching. Then it occurred to me: 'Rāma did not
proclaim "I live having realized this teaching with my own higher knowing,
having entered into it" by mere faith alone — surely he lived knowing and
seeing this teaching.' So I approached Uddaka, son of Rāma, and asked:
"Reverend, up to what point did Rāma proclaim that he had realized this
teaching with his own higher knowing and entered into it?"

When I said this, he declared the sphere of neither-recognition-nor-non-recognition.

Then it occurred to me: 'It was not only Rāma who had confidence — I too have
confidence. It was not only Rāma who had energy, remembering, mental composure,
and discernment — I too have these. What if I were to make the effort to
realize the teaching that Rāma proclaims he had realized with his own higher
knowing?'

Soon enough, I too realized that teaching with my own higher knowing and
entered into it. I went to Uddaka, son of Rāma, and said: "Reverend, did Rāma
realize this teaching with his own higher knowing up to this point and enter
into it?"

"He did, reverend."

"I too, reverend, have realized this teaching with my own higher knowing up to
this point and live having entered into it."

"We are fortunate, reverend — how very fortunate — to see such a venerable as
yourself as a fellow practitioner! The teaching that Rāma realized with his
own higher knowing and entered into — that you live having realized with your
own higher knowing. The teaching that you live having realized with your own
higher knowing — that Rāma realized and made known. What Rāma knew, you know;
what you know, Rāma knew. As Rāma was, so are you; as you are, so was Rāma.
Come now, reverend — you should lead this community."

And so Uddaka, son of Rāma — my fellow practitioner — placed me in the
position of teacher and honored me with high honor.

Then it occurred to me: 'This teaching does not lead to disenchantment, fading,
cessation, calming, higher knowing, awakening, or nibbāna — only as far as
rebirth in the sphere of neither-recognition-nor-non-recognition.'

Not finding this teaching satisfying, I turned away from it and left.

## Arrival at Uruvelā and Awakening

Still in search of the good, seeking the supreme resting-place of peace, I
traveled stage by stage through the Magadhan lands until I arrived at the town
of Senā in Uruvelā. There I saw a delightful stretch of ground, a beautiful
grove with a flowing river, clean and charming, with smooth and pleasant banks,
and nearby a village to go to for alms.

Then it occurred to me: 'This is truly a delightful stretch of ground — a
beautiful grove with a flowing river, clean and charming, with smooth and
pleasant banks, and nearby a village to go to for alms. This is good enough
for striving, for a person of good family intent on striving.' And so I sat
down right there, thinking: 'This is good enough for striving.'

Being myself subject to birth, having seen the danger in what is subject to
birth, I sought nibbāna — the supreme security from the yoke, free from birth
— and I found it. Being myself subject to aging, having seen the danger in what
is subject to aging, I sought nibbāna — the supreme security from the yoke,
free from aging — and I found it. Being myself subject to sickness, having seen
the danger in what is subject to sickness, I sought nibbāna — the supreme
security from the yoke, free from sickness — and I found it. Being myself
subject to death, having seen the danger in what is subject to death, I sought
nibbāna — the supreme security from the yoke, free from death — and I found
it. Being myself subject to sorrow, having seen the danger in what is subject
to sorrow, I sought nibbāna — the supreme security from the yoke, free from
sorrow — and I found it. Being myself subject to corruption, having seen the
danger in what is subject to corruption, I sought nibbāna — the supreme
security from the yoke, free from corruption — and I found it.

Knowledge and vision arose in me: 'My release is unshakable. This is my last
birth. There is no more further becoming.'

## Hesitation

Then it occurred to me: 'This teaching I have reached is deep, hard to see,
hard to realize, peaceful, refined, beyond the scope of thought, subtle, to be
experienced by the wise. But this generation delights in its resting-place,
is pleased with its resting-place, rejoices in its resting-place. It is hard
for this generation to see this truth: conditionality, dependent arising. And
this too is hard to see: the calming of all putting-things-together, the
relinquishing of all supports, the ending of ignorant wanting, fading,
cessation, nibbāna. If I were to teach this Dhamma and others did not
understand me, that would be wearisome and troublesome for me.'

And then these verses, unheard before, arose in me spontaneously:

> Struggled hard have I for this attainment —  
> enough, now, to make it known.  
> Those overcome by passion and aversion  
> will not easily understand this teaching.  
> Going against the stream, subtle,  
> deep, hard to see, and fine —  
> those inflamed by passion will not see it,  
> veiled as they are in a mass of darkness.

As I reflected in this way, my mind inclined toward remaining at ease, not
toward teaching the Dhamma.

## Brahmā Sahampati's Request

Then Brahmā Sahampati, knowing my train of thought, thought: 'The world will
be lost! The world will perish! For the mind of the Tathāgata, the arahant,
the perfectly and fully awakened one, inclines toward remaining at ease, not
toward teaching the Dhamma.'

Then, as quickly as a strong person might extend a bent arm or bend an
extended arm, Brahmā Sahampati vanished from the Brahmā-world and appeared
before me. He arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his cupped hands
toward me, and said: "Bhante, let the Buddha teach the Dhamma! Let the
Well-Departed One teach the Dhamma! There are beings with little dust in their
eyes who are declining for lack of hearing the Dhamma. There will be those who
understand the Dhamma!"

That is what Brahmā Sahampati said. Then he said further:

> Among the Magadhans there appeared in the past > a teaching thought up by
those stained with impurity. > Open wide the door to the deathless! > Let them
hear the Dhamma found by the stainless one. > > As someone standing on a rocky
summit > can see the people all around — > so too, Wise One, All-Seeing, >
ascending the palace of Dhamma, > look upon the people swamped in sorrow, >
yourself sorrowless, overcome by birth and aging. > > Rise, hero! Victor in
battle, > caravan-leader, free of debt, wander the world. > Let the Buddha
teach the Dhamma — > there will be those who understand!

## The Lotus Simile

Then, understanding Brahmā's invitation and out of compassion for beings, I
surveyed the world with the eye of a Buddha.

Surveying with the eye of a Buddha, I saw beings with little dust in their
eyes and with much dust in their eyes; with keen faculties and with dull
faculties; with good qualities and with bad qualities; easy to teach and hard
to teach; some living seeing the danger of faults in another world, and some
not.

Just as in a pool of blue lotuses, or pink lotuses, or white lotuses, some
lotuses are born and grow in the water, stay below the surface, and flourish
submerged; some are born and grow in the water, stand even with the surface;
and some are born and grow in the water but rise up above the surface and stand
untouched by the water — in the same way, surveying the world with the eye of
a Buddha, I saw beings with little dust in their eyes and with much dust in
their eyes, with keen faculties and with dull faculties, easy to teach and hard
to teach.

I replied to Brahmā Sahampati in verse:

> Open are the doors to the deathless —  
> let those with ears commit to confidence.  
> Thinking it would be wearisome, Brahmā,  
> I did not readily teach the refined Dhamma among humans.

Then Brahmā Sahampati, knowing that his request for the teaching of the Dhamma
had been granted, bowed to me and circumambulated me with his right side
toward me, and vanished right there.

## Who to Teach First

Then it occurred to me: 'To whom should I first teach the Dhamma? Who will
quickly understand this teaching?' Then I thought: 'Āḷāra Kālāma is wise,
capable, discerning, and for a long time has had little dust in his eyes. Why
not teach him first? He will quickly understand this teaching.'

But a deity came and told me: 'Bhante, Āḷāra Kālāma passed away seven days
ago.' And knowledge and vision arose in me: 'Āḷāra Kālāma passed away seven
days ago.'

I thought: 'This is a great loss for Āḷāra Kālāma. If he had heard this
teaching, he would have understood it quickly.'

Then it occurred to me again: 'To whom should I first teach the Dhamma? Who
will quickly understand this teaching?' Then I thought: 'Uddaka, son of Rāma,
is wise, capable, discerning, and for a long time has had little dust in his
eyes. Why not teach him first? He will quickly understand this teaching.'

But a deity came and told me: 'Bhante, Uddaka, son of Rāma, passed away just
last night.' And knowledge and vision arose in me: 'Uddaka, son of Rāma,
passed away just last night.'

I thought: 'This is a great loss for Uddaka. If he had heard this teaching, he
would have understood it quickly.'

Then it occurred to me again: 'To whom should I first teach the Dhamma? Who
will quickly understand this teaching?' Then I thought: 'The group of five
bhikkhus was very helpful to me — they attended to me during my time of
resolute striving. Why not teach them first?' Then I wondered: 'Where are the
group of five bhikkhus staying now?'

With the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, I saw the group of
five bhikkhus staying near Vārāṇasī, in the deer park at Isipatana. So, when
I had stayed in Uruvelā as long as I wished, I set out for Vārāṇasī.

## Upaka the Ājīvaka

While I was traveling along the road between Gayā and the place of awakening,
the wanderer Upaka of the Ājīvaka sect saw me. He said: "Reverend, your
faculties are very clear, your complexion is pure and bright. In whose name
have you gone forth, reverend? Who is your teacher? Whose Dhamma do you
approve of?"

I replied to Upaka in verse:

> I am the all-conqueror, the knower of all,  
> unstained in the midst of all things.  
> Having given up all, freed through the ending of ignorant wanting —  
> having known this for myself, whose follower should I be?  
>  
> I have no teacher;  
> there is no one like me.  
> In the world with its gods  
> there is no equal to me.  
>  
> For I am the arahant in the world,  
> I am the unsurpassed teacher.  
> I alone am perfectly and fully awakened,  
> cooled, quenched.  
>  
> To set rolling the Wheel of Dhamma  
> I go to the city of Kāsi.  
> In a world gone blind  
> I shall beat the drum of the deathless.

Upaka said: "According to what you claim, reverend, you ought to be the
Infinite Victor."

> Those like me are victors —  
> they who have reached the ending of outflows.  
> Unwholesome qualities are conquered by me —  
> that is why, Upaka, I am a victor.

When I had spoken, Upaka said: "So be it, reverend," shook his head, took the
wrong road, and left.

## The Five Ascetics

Traveling stage by stage, I arrived at Vārāṇasī, at the deer park at Isipatana,
and went to where the group of five bhikkhus was staying. The group of five
bhikkhus saw me coming from a distance. Seeing me, they agreed among
themselves: "Here comes the recluse Gotama — he gave up the struggle and turned
to abundance. We should not bow to him or rise for him or take his bowl and
robe. But we can set out a seat; if he wishes, he can sit."

Yet as I drew near, the group of five bhikkhus found themselves unable to hold
to their agreement. Some came to meet me and took my bowl and robe; some set
out a seat; some set out water for washing feet. They addressed me by name,
however, and as "reverend."

So I said to them: "Bhikkhus, do not address the Tathāgata by name and as
'reverend.' The Tathāgata is an arahant, perfectly and fully awakened. Listen,
bhikkhus: the deathless has been reached! I shall instruct you. I shall teach
you the Dhamma. Practicing as instructed, you will soon, in this very life,
realize with your own higher knowing the supreme culmination of the spiritual
life — that for which gentlemen rightly go forth from home into homelessness
— and live having entered into it."

But the bhikkhus said to me: "Reverend Gotama, even by that conduct, that
practice, that grueling austerity, you did not reach any superhuman distinction
in knowledge and vision worthy of a noble one. How will you reach it now that
you have turned to abundance and given up the struggle?"

I said: "Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata has not turned to abundance, has not given
up the struggle. The Tathāgata is an arahant, perfectly and fully awakened.
Listen, bhikkhus: the deathless has been reached! I shall instruct you. I
shall teach you the Dhamma. Practicing as instructed, you will soon realize
the supreme culmination of the spiritual life and live having entered into it."

A second time the bhikkhus said the same. A second time I replied in the same
way.

A third time the bhikkhus said: "Reverend Gotama, even by that conduct, that
practice, that grueling austerity, you did not reach any superhuman distinction
in knowledge and vision worthy of a noble one. How will you reach it now that
you have turned to abundance and given up the struggle?"

I said to them: "Bhikkhus, have you ever known me to speak like this before?"

"No, Bhante."

"The Tathāgata is an arahant, perfectly and fully awakened. Listen, bhikkhus:
the deathless has been reached! I shall instruct you. I shall teach you the
Dhamma. Practicing as instructed, you will soon, in this very life, realize
with your own higher knowing the supreme culmination of the spiritual life —
that for which gentlemen rightly go forth from home into homelessness — and
live having entered into it."

I was able to bring the group of five bhikkhus around. Then sometimes I would
instruct two bhikkhus while the other three went on alms-round, and we six
would live on what those three brought back. Sometimes I would instruct three
bhikkhus while the other two went on alms-round, and we six would live on
what those two brought back.

## The Five Achieve the Noble Search

As the group of five bhikkhus was being instructed and guided by me in this
way, being themselves subject to birth, having seen the danger in what is
subject to birth, they sought nibbāna — the supreme security from the yoke,
free from birth — and they found it. Being themselves subject to aging, having
seen the danger in what is subject to aging, they sought nibbāna — the supreme
security from the yoke, free from aging — and they found it. Being themselves
subject to sickness, death, sorrow, and corruption, having seen the danger in
these, they sought nibbāna — the supreme security from the yoke, free from
sickness, death, sorrow, and corruption — and they found it.

Knowledge and vision arose in them: 'Our release is unshakable. This is our
last birth. There is no more further becoming.'

## Sensual Pleasure and the Snare

Bhikkhus, there are five strands of sensual pleasure. What five? Sights
cognized by the eye that are desired, agreeable, pleasing, of a pleasant
nature, connected to sensual pleasure, arousing; sounds cognized by the ear;
smells cognized by the nose; tastes cognized by the tongue; touches cognized
by the body that are desired, agreeable, pleasing, of a pleasant nature,
connected to sensual pleasure, arousing. These are the five strands of sensual
pleasure.

Those recluses or brahmins who indulge in these five strands of sensual
pleasure tied, infatuated, and immersed in them, not seeing the danger, without
the discernment of escape — they should be understood as: having met with
calamity and disaster, subject to the Wicked Their will.

Suppose a wild deer was lying in the wilderness caught on a heap of snares. It
should be understood as: having met with calamity and disaster, subject to the
hunter's will. And when the hunter arrives, it cannot go wherever it wishes.

In the same way, those recluses or brahmins who indulge in these five strands
of sensual pleasure tied, infatuated, and immersed in them, not seeing the
danger, without the discernment of escape — they should be understood as:
having met with calamity and disaster, subject to the Wicked Their will.

Those recluses or brahmins, however, who indulge in these five strands of
sensual pleasure without being tied, infatuated, or immersed in them, seeing
the danger, with the discernment of escape — they should be understood as:
having not met with calamity and disaster, not subject to the Wicked Their
will.

Suppose a wild deer was lying in the wilderness on a heap of snares without
being caught. It should be understood as: having not met with calamity and
disaster, not subject to the hunter's will. And when the hunter arrives, it
can go wherever it wishes.

In the same way, those recluses or brahmins who indulge in these five strands
of sensual pleasure without being tied, infatuated, or immersed in them, seeing
the danger, with the discernment of escape — they should be understood as:
having not met with calamity and disaster, not subject to the Wicked Their
will.

Suppose a wild deer were wandering in the forest, walking, standing, sitting,
and lying down in confidence. Why? Because it is beyond the hunter's range.

## Blinding Māra: The Mental Themes and Beyond

In the same way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu — secluded from sense pleasures, secluded
from unwholesome qualities — enters and remains in the first mental theme, with
placing the mind, keeping it there, with rejoicing and satisfaction born of
seclusion.

This bhikkhu is said to have blinded Māra, to have put out Māra's eye without
a trace, and to have gone where the Wicked One cannot see.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, with the settling of placing and keeping the mind,
internally confident, with a unified feeling mind, without placing and keeping
the mind, a bhikkhu enters and remains in the second mental theme with
rejoicing and satisfaction born of mental composure.

This bhikkhu is said to have blinded Māra, to have put out Māra's eye without
a trace, and to have gone where the Wicked One cannot see.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, with the fading of rejoicing, a bhikkhu remains
equanimous, remembering and clearly knowing, and experiences satisfaction with
the body — what the noble ones speak of as 'equanimous, remembering, living
well' — and enters and remains in the third mental theme.

This bhikkhu is said to have blinded Māra, to have put out Māra's eye without
a trace, and to have gone where the Wicked One cannot see.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, with the abandoning of satisfaction and distress, and
with the prior ending of gladness and grief, a bhikkhu enters and remains in
the fourth mental theme — neither satisfaction nor distress, with purity of
equanimity and remembering.

This bhikkhu is said to have blinded Māra, to have put out Māra's eye without
a trace, and to have gone where the Wicked One cannot see.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, with the complete transcending of perceptions of form,
with the passing away of perceptions of resistance, with non-attention to
perceptions of diversity, aware that 'space is boundless,' a bhikkhu enters
and remains in the sphere of boundless space.

This bhikkhu is said to have blinded Māra, to have put out Māra's eye without
a trace, and to have gone where the Wicked One cannot see.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, going completely beyond the sphere of boundless space,
aware that 'knowing is boundless,' a bhikkhu enters and remains in the sphere
of boundless knowing.

This bhikkhu is said to have blinded Māra, to have put out Māra's eye without
a trace, and to have gone where the Wicked One cannot see.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, going completely beyond the sphere of boundless knowing,
aware that 'there is nothing at all,' a bhikkhu enters and remains in the
sphere of nothingness.

This bhikkhu is said to have blinded Māra, to have put out Māra's eye without
a trace, and to have gone where the Wicked One cannot see.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, going completely beyond the sphere of nothingness, a
bhikkhu enters and remains in the sphere of neither-recognition-nor-non-recognition.

This bhikkhu is said to have blinded Māra, to have put out Māra's eye without
a trace, and to have gone where the Wicked One cannot see.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, going completely beyond the sphere of
neither-recognition-nor-non-recognition, a bhikkhu enters and remains in the
cessation of recognition and felt experience. And having seen with discernment,
their outflows are exhausted.

This bhikkhu is said to have blinded Māra, to have put out Māra's eye without a
trace, and to have gone where the Wicked One cannot see. They have crossed over
the world's entanglement. They walk, stand, sit, and lie down in confidence.
Why? Because they are beyond the Wicked Their range."

That is what the Buddha said. Satisfied, those bhikkhus approved of the
Buddha's words.

The sixth discourse is finished.

---

[← The Man Struck by a Poisoned Arrow](mn63-culamalukya-sutta.md) · [All suttas](index.md) · [The First Teaching →](sn56-11-dhammacakkappavattana-sutta.md)


*[Bhante]: A respectful way of addressing a senior monastic, roughly "venerable sir." Left untranslated because English has no natural equivalent.
*[Dhamma]: The Buddha's teaching taken as a whole -- both what he taught and the way things actually are, which the teaching describes.
*[Tathāgata]: A title for the Buddha, traditionally left untranslated. It means roughly "the one who has arrived at things as they truly are."
*[arahant]: Someone who has completed the path and has nothing further to do. Left untranslated; "saint" and "perfected one" both mislead.
*[aversion]: One of the three "roots" behind unwholesome action, alongside greed and delusion -- the pushback against what's unwanted or unpleasant.
*[awakening]: Coming fully awake to how things are. Sometimes translated "enlightenment," a word this project avoids as needlessly mystical.
*[bhikkhu]: A Buddhist monk -- someone who has left household life to practise full time. Left untranslated because "monk" carries centuries of unrelated European associations.
*[bhikkhus]: Buddhist monks -- those who have left household life to practise full time. The Buddha's usual way of addressing the assembly, roughly "friends" in force.
*[birth]: This project's rendering of "jāti" -- being born, and the link that ageing and dying depend on in the dependent-arising sequence. In MN 141 the word appears once in its everyday sense instead, in a simile about a mother.
*[body]: The physical body. In MN 63 specifically, paired with "soul" in one of the undeclared questions.
*[brahmin]: A member of the hereditary priestly class of ancient India. In these texts it usually appears in the stock pair "ascetics and brahmins," which means religious teachers and practitioners in general rather than one caste.
*[calming]: A settling and quieting of the mind on the way toward full release.
*[cessation]: The ending of dissatisfaction and its causes -- what practice is ultimately for. (Elsewhere on this site the same underlying idea is called "quenching" -- both are this project's rendering of the same Pali word, "nirodha," used in different sentences.)
*[clearly knowing]: Acting while plainly aware of what you are doing.
*[dependent arising]: The teaching that experience -- and the dissatisfaction in it -- comes from conditions rather than from any fixed self or essence. Each link depends on the one before it, which is why removing a condition stops what follows.
*[disenchantment]: A cooling of fascination with ordinary experience -- not depression, but the natural next step once you see clearly how things actually work.
*[escape]: A genuine way out of being stuck in a feeling -- as opposed to the false escapes (like chasing pleasure) an untrained mind tends to reach for instead.
*[fading]: The fading away of attraction and investment in experience, as passion cools.
*[feeling mind]: This project's rendering of "citta" -- the mind as the part of you that feels, wants, and reacts, and the part that can be trained, settled, and freed. Closer to "heart" in everyday English than to "intellect."
*[felt experience]: This project's rendering of "vedanā" (often translated "feeling") -- the immediate pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral tone of an experience, prior to any story built on top of it.
*[form]: This project's rendering of "rūpa" -- the physical, material aspect of experience, one of the five heaps.
*[gladness]: This project's rendering of "muditā" (often translated "sympathetic joy") -- being genuinely glad at someone else's good fortune, cultivated as a practice rather than assumed to come naturally.
*[higher knowing]: Direct, personally realized understanding -- not a special power, just knowing something for yourself rather than taking it on faith.
*[ignorant wanting]: This project's rendering of "taṇhā" (often translated "craving"), chosen to keep visible that the wanting in question is driven by not seeing clearly, not just ordinary desire.
*[knowing]: This project's rendering of "viññāṇa" (often translated "consciousness") -- bare awareness of an object through one of the senses or the mind.
*[mental composure]: This project's rendering of "samādhi" -- a collected, settled, workable state of mind. Usually translated "concentration," which this project avoids because it suggests forcing and strain.
*[mental theme]: This project's rendering of "jhāna" -- a single theme the mind rests on and holds steadily. Described in a sequence of four, each calmer than the last. Most translations leave the word in Pāli.
*[nibbāna]: The end of greed, hatred, and confusion -- the traditional goal of Buddhist practice. Left untranslated because no single English word covers it; "quenching" is the closest one-word gloss.
*[outflows]: This project's rendering of "āsavā" -- deep-running habits that keep seeping out and driving behaviour, classically sensuality, becoming, and ignorance. Often translated "taints" or "defilements."
*[recognition]: This project's rendering of "saññā" (often translated "perception") -- the mind's act of identifying and labeling what it encounters.
*[resistance]: A reflexive pushing-away from what's unwanted, arising automatically in response to unpleasant feeling.
*[sphere of boundless knowing]: A deep meditative state in which awareness rests on knowing itself without limit.
*[sphere of boundless space]: A deep meditative state in which awareness rests on space without limit.
*[sphere of nothingness]: A deep meditative state in which awareness rests on there being nothing at all to take up.
*[spiritual life]: The Buddhist path of practice as a whole -- not just a set of beliefs, but a whole way of living.
*[unwholesome]: This project's rendering of "akusala" -- roughly, mentally and ethically harmful: blameworthy, leads to harm, and is criticized by people with good judgment.
*[world]: A common word in these texts that shifts meaning by context -- sometimes the physical cosmos beings are reborn into, sometimes (as in MN 63) a specific philosophical question about whether existence as a whole is eternal or finite. Each sutta's own framing makes clear which sense is meant.
